o: En un lugar de la Mancha, de cuyo nombre no quiero acordarme, no ha mucho tiempo que vivía un hidalgo de los de lanza en astillero, adarga antigua, rocín flaco y galgo corredor.
t: In a place in La Mancha, whose name I have no wish to recall, not long ago there lived a gentleman of the sort they call lance-and-stocking, old galley, lean nag, and greyhound.

o: Una olla de algo más vaca que carnero, salpicón las más noches, duelos y quebrantos los sábados, lantejas los viernes, algún palomino de añadidura los domingos, consumían las tres partes de su hacienda.
t: A stew of something more beef than mutton, scraps most nights, duels and feasts on Saturdays, lentils on Fridays, some extra squab on Sundays, consumed three parts of his fortune.

o: El resto della concluían sayo de velarte, calzas de velludo para las fiestas, con sus pantuflos de lo mesmo, y los días de entresemana se honraba con su vellorí de lo más fino.
t: The rest of it they made up with jerkin of fine cloth, velvet breeches for the holidays, with slippers to match, and on weekdays they did themselves honour with a jerkin of the finest.

o: Tenía en su casa una ama que pasaba de los cuarenta, y una sobrina que no llegaba a los veinte, y un mozo de campo y plaza, que así ensillaba el rocín como tomaba la podadera.
t: He had in his house a housekeeper past forty, and a niece not yet twenty, and a lad from the field and the square, who saddled the nag as deftly as he took the pruning hook.

o: Frisaba la edad de nuestro hidalgo con los cincuenta años; era de complexión recia, seco de carnes, enjuto de rostro, gran madrugador y amigo de la caza.
t: Our gentleman's age was about fifty; he was of a tough constitution, spare of flesh, lean of face, an early riser, and a lover of the chase.

o: Quieren decir que tenía el sobrenombre de Quijada, o Quesada, que en esto hay alguna diferencia en los autores que deste caso escriben; aunque, por conjeturas verosímiles, se deja entender que se llamaba Quejana.
t: They say that he had the nickname of Quijada, or Quesada, and in this there is some difference among the authors who have written of this case; though, by plausible conjecture, it may be gathered that his name was Quejana.

o: Pero esto importa poco a nuestro cuento; basta que en la narración dél no se salga un punto de la verdad.
t: But this matters little to our tale; it is enough that in the telling of it not a point of the truth be departed from.

o: Es, pues, de saber que este sobredicho hidalgo, los ratos que estaba ocioso, que eran los más del año, se daba a leer libros de caballerías, con tanta afición y gusto, que olvidó casi de todo punto el ejercicio de la caza, y aun la administración de su hacienda.
t: So it is to be known that this aforementioned gentleman, in his idle moments, which were most of the year, gave himself to reading books of chivalry with such relish and pleasure that he well-nigh forgot the exercise of the chase, and even the management of his estate.

o: Y también cuando leía: ...los altos cielos que de vuestra divinidad divinamente con las estrellas os fortifican, y os hacen merecedora del merecimiento que merece la vuestra grandeza.
t: And when he read: "...the high heavens that with the stars divinely fortify your divinity, and make you worthy of the merit that your greatness deserves."

o: Con estas razones perdía el pobre caballero el juicio, y desvelábase por entenderlas y desentrañarles el sentido, que no se lo sacara ni las entendiera el mesmo Aristóteles, si resucitara para sólo ello.
t: With these words the poor knight lost his reason, and lay awake trying to understand them and to wrest their meaning from them, which neither Aristotle himself, if he should rise again for that purpose alone, could have extracted or understood.

o: No estaba muy bien con las heridas que don Belianís daba y recebía, porque se imaginaba que, por grandes maestros que le hubiesen curado, no dejaría de tener el rostro y todo el cuerpo lleno de cicatrices y señales.
t: He was not on good terms with the wounds that Don Belianis gave and received, for he fancied that, however great masters might have healed him, he would still be covered with scars and marks on his face and all over his body.

o: Pero, con todo, alababa en su autor aquel acabar su libro con la promesa de aquella inacabable aventura, y muchas veces le vino deseo de tomar la pluma y dalle fin al pie de la letra, como allí se promete; y sin duda alguna lo hiciera, y aun saliera con ello, si otros mayores y continuos pensamientos no se lo estorbaran.
t: Yet, for all that, he praised in his author the ending of his book with the promise of that unending adventure, and many a time he felt a desire to take up the pen and finish it to the letter, as is there promised; and beyond doubt he would have done so, and would have come out of it with credit, if other greater and more continual thoughts had not stood in his way.

o: En resolución, él se enfrascó tanto en su letura, que se le pasaban las noches leyendo de claro en claro, y los días de turbio en turbio; y así, del poco dormir y del mucho leer, se le secó el celebro, de manera que vino a perder el juicio.
t: In short, he became so absorbed in his reading that the nights passed as he read on from light to light, and the days from dark to dark; and so, from little sleep and much reading, his brain dried up, in such a way that he came to lose his reason.

o: Decía él que el Cid Ruy Díaz había sido muy buen caballero, pero que no tenía que ver con el Caballero de la Ardiente Espada, que de sólo un revés había partido por medio dos fieros y descomunales gigantes.
t: He would say that Cid Ruy Díaz had been a very good knight, but that he had nothing to do with the Knight of the Burning Sword, who with a single backhand stroke had cleft in twain two fierce and monstrous giants.

o: Mejor estaba con Bernardo del Carpio, porque en Roncesvalles había muerto a Roldán el encantado, valiéndose de la industria de Hércules, cuando ahogó a Anteo, el hijo de la Tierra, entre los brazos.
t: He was better satisfied with Bernardo del Carpio, because at Roncesvalles he had slain the enchanted Roland, availing himself of the craft of Hercules, when he drowned Antaeus, the son of the Earth, in his arms.

o: Decía mucho bien del gigante Morgante, porque, con ser de aquella generación gigantea, que todos son soberbios y descomedidos, él solo era afable y bien criado.
t: He spoke very well of the giant Morgante, because, though he belonged to that giant generation, which are all proud and overbearing, he alone was affable and well bred.

o: Pero, sobre todos, estaba bien con Reinaldos de Montalbán, y más cuando le veía salir de su castillo y robar cuantos topaba, y cuando en allende robó aquel ídolo de Mahoma que era todo de oro, según dice su historia.
t: But above all he was well disposed toward Reinaldos of Montalbán, and most of all when he saw him sallying from his castle and robbing everyone he met, and when beyond the seas he robbed that idol of Mahomet which was all of gold, as his history tells.

o: Diera él, por dar una mano de coces al traidor de Galalón, al ama que tenía, y aun a su sobrina de añadidura.
t: He would have given, for giving a helping hand to the traitor of Galalón, his housekeeper, and his niece into the bargain.

o: Imaginábase el pobre ya coronado por el valor de su brazo, por lo menos, del imperio de Trapisonda; y así, con estos tan agradables pensamientos, llevado del estraño gusto que en ellos sentía, se dio priesa a poner en efeto lo que deseaba.
t: The poor man fancied himself already crowned, at the very least, by the valour of his arm, over the empire of Trebizond; and so, with these pleasant thoughts, carried away by the strange delight he felt in them, he set to work to put into effect what he desired.

o: Y lo primero que hizo fue limpiar unas armas que habían sido de sus bisabuelos, que, tomadas de orín y llenas de moho, luengos siglos había que estaban puestas y olvidadas en un rincón.
t: And the first thing he did was to clean some armour that had belonged to his great-grandfathers, which, rust-stained and covered with mould, had lain for ages forgotten in a corner.

o: Limpiólas y aderezólas lo mejor que pudo, pero vio que tenían una gran falta, y era que no tenían celada de encaje, sino morrión simple; mas a esto suplió su industria, porque de cartones hizo un modo de media celada, que, encajada con el morrión, hacían una apariencia de celada entera.
t: He cleaned them up and fitted them out as best he could, but he saw they had a great shortcoming: they had no visor of mail, only a simple morion; but he made up for this with his ingenuity, for out of cardboard he fashioned a sort of half-visor which, fitted onto the morion, gave the appearance of a complete visor.

o: Fue luego a ver su rocín, y, aunque tenía más cuartos que un real y más tachas que el caballo de Gonela, que tantum pellis et ossa fuit, le pareció que ni el Bucéfalo de Alejandro ni Babieca el del Cid con él se igualaban.
t: He then went to look at his nag, and, though it had more ribs than a rial and more flaws than Gonela's horse, which tantum pellis et ossa fuit, it seemed to him that neither Alexander's Bucephalus nor the Cid's Babieca could compare with it.

o: Y así, después de muchos nombres que formó, borró y quitó, añadió, deshizo y tornó a hacer en su memoria e imaginación, al fin le vino a llamar Rocinante: nombre, a su parecer, alto, sonoro y significativo de lo que había sido cuando fue rocín, antes de lo que ahora era, que era antes y primero de todos los rocines del mundo.
t: And so, after many names he invented, erased, discarded, added, undid, and made over again in his mind and imagination, at last it came to him to call it Rocinante: a name, in his opinion, lofty, sonorous, and significant of what it had been when it was a nag, before what it now was, which was before and above all the nags in the world.

o: Puesto nombre, y tan a su gusto, a su caballo, quiso ponérsele a sí mismo, y en este pensamiento duró otros ocho días, y al cabo se vino a llamar don Quijote; de donde —como queda dicho— tomaron ocasión los autores desta tan verdadera historia que, sin duda, se debía de llamar Quijada, y no Quesada, como otros quisieron decir.
t: Having named his horse, and to his own liking so well, he wanted to give himself a name too, and in this thought he spent another eight days, and at the end he came to call himself Don Quixote; whence—as has been said—the authors of this so true history took occasion to say that without a doubt it should have been called Quijada, and not Quesada, as others would have it.

o: Limpias, pues, sus armas, hecho del morrión celada, puesto nombre a su rocín y confirmándose a sí mismo, se dio a entender que no le faltaba otra cosa sino buscar una dama de quien enamorarse; porque el caballero andante sin amores era árbol sin hojas y sin fruto y cuerpo sin alma. Decíase él a sí.
t: Having therefore cleaned his weapons, made a visor out of his morion, named his nag, and confirmed himself in his own mind, he came to believe that all that was left for him was to seek out a lady of whom to fall in love; for a knight-errant without love was a tree without leaves or fruit, a body without a soul. Thus he said to himself.

o: ¡Oh, cómo se holgó nuestro buen caballero cuando hubo hecho este discurso, y más cuando halló a quien dar nombre de su dama!
t: Oh, how our good knight rejoiced when he had made this speech, and even more when he found someone to whom he could give the name of his lady!

o: Y fue, a lo que se cree, que en un lugar cerca del suyo había una moza labradora de muy buen parecer, de quien él un tiempo anduvo enamorado, aunque, según se entiende, ella jamás lo supo, ni le dio cata dello.
t: It is generally believed that in a place near his own there was a farm girl of very good looks, of whom he was for a time enamoured, though, as is understood, she never knew it, nor gave him so much as a glance.
